extracted.intended_audience: public relations practitioners and students; corporate communications and advertising managers
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on planning, executing, and evaluating corporate and advocacy public-relations advertising (print, broadcast, and direct) and related management choices (including lobbying/advocacy positioning). Focuses on objectives, audience/medium selection, ad elements, evaluation, budgeting, and campaign purpose (symmetric vs asymmetric).

rubrics_metrics.name: When to choose paid advertising (management consideration)
rubrics_metrics.description: Organizations choose paid advertisements as a public relations medium when they want access to the media and want to control the content of the message they communicate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Most often used in public affairs/government relations, community relations, and economic education programs. Used as substitute for or complement to press relations when media do not put the organization on public agendas. Advertising gives control over content and access to audiences the media may otherwise block.

rubrics_metrics.name: Primary realistic objectives for issues advertising
rubrics_metrics.description: For issues advertisements, the manager should first strive for readership of the ad (communication objective) and retention of the organization's message.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Message acceptance (seeing the issue as the organization sees it) and favorable attitudes/supportive behavior are possible but uncommon. The most realistic acceptance strategy is hedging (audiences combine ad cognitions with other sources). Campaigns more often reduce opposing behaviors than produce supportive behaviors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Primary objectives for organizational identity advertising
rubrics_metrics.description: For organizational identity advertising, objectives should be exposure (communication) and message retention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These ads target passive publics (especially on television) so the realistic aim is for passive publics to know the organization exists and associate it with certain traits. Any additional objective beyond exposure and retention is generally unrealistic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be cautious in choosing objectives
rubrics_metrics.description: Advertising managers must set realistic, medium-appropriate objectives and prioritize readership/viewership and retention over expecting wholesale attitude or behavior change from a single ad.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize hedging and wedging effects; design objectives around what the medium and audience realistically permit; use formative research to set objectives and test appeals before full campaign commitment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluation measures for advertising effectiveness
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate campaigns via readership/viewership, message retention, message acceptance (including hedging/wedging), attitudes, and behaviors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use telephone or personal interviews with target publics. First establish exposure (did they read/view the ad?), then measure retention and acceptance; for behavior effects, measure response actions. The chapter refers to the measures outlined in Chapter 9 and recommends these empirical steps.

rubrics_metrics.name: Advertising cost and budgeting considerations
rubrics_metrics.description: Advertising is expensive to produce and place; budget carefully and weigh costs against benefits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do formative research on sample publics before committing to a full campaign. Use time-budgeting techniques and the simplified programming technique (see Chap. 8) to organize program and schedules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Determine audience and goals before designing ad
rubrics_metrics.description: Begin the design of a corporate advertisement by determining the audience to be reached and the goals to be served; then conduct careful research to marshal facts and select the strongest points before turning to layout.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Audience/activity level (passive vs active), objectives (exposure vs acceptance), and research findings should drive message strategy and media choice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Elements of the print advertisement (five components)
rubrics_metrics.description: A newspaper or magazine advertisement should include five components: headline, copy, art (illustration), signature/logo with address, and white space.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Headline: grabs attention and poses a question or proposition to entice further reading. Copy: develops the headline premise and leads to desired conclusion. Art: attracts attention and appeals to emotions. Signature/logo/address: identifies sponsor and provides contact for more information. White space: directs the eye, separates the ad from surrounding content, and relieves clutter to aid readability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Elements and constraints of broadcast ads
rubrics_metrics.description: Broadcast ads are linear and time‑bound; the creator must allocate seconds for attention-getting, theme development, and call-to-action, and can use sound and motion to enhance realism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Television permits both action and print (freeze-frame final frame with logo/slogan/address), and layering (voice-over plus visuals). Sound effects and voice selection are critical — they 'grab us by the collar' and can annoy, surprise, or convince. Radio lacks visuals but listeners create the image mentally; radio generally requires frequent repetition and tends to plant a single idea or fact that can be augmented by print.

rubrics_metrics.name: Select medium by publics' activity level
rubrics_metrics.description: Publics vary by advertising medium: television most often reaches passive publics; print ads generally reach active publics (readers who choose to read an ad).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Concentrate issues advertising in newspapers and national newsmagazines read by active publics (e.g., New York/Washington papers) when targeting people involved with national policy issues. Use TV identity ads to reach passive audiences for name/trait recognition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Direct advertising for eliciting public action
rubrics_metrics.description: If publics are expected to contribute to a cause, join an organization, send for information, or cast a vote, mass-media advertising may be insufficient and direct-mail advertising is necessary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Direct mail allows longer, personalized messages (multipage personal letters, brochures, return envelopes), segmentation of publics with tailored appeals, and tracking/counting of responses to measure effectiveness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design of broadcast timing and sequencing
rubrics_metrics.description: In broadcast ads the creator must decide exactly how many seconds should be devoted to capturing attention, developing and supporting a theme, and summarizing or calling for action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plan linear flow because viewers/listeners cannot control pacing. Use appropriate sequencing to balance attention-getting and message development. Shorter follow-up spots (30s/20s) can continue a campaign beginning with 60s spots.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of persuasive devices and appeals in takeover/controversial campaigns
rubrics_metrics.description: When ownership or control is at stake, every persuasive device can be useful: rational appeals (long explanations in news/business pages) and blunt emotional appeals (short bold ads) both have roles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose appeal and placement according to target audience (e.g., detailed rational appeals to investors in business sections; emotional appeals to employees emphasizing pride/patriotism). Placement (news vs business section) and ad voice (management vs employees) affect positioning and effectiveness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Advocacy advertising — four reasons (Sethi)
rubrics_metrics.description: Corporations use advocacy advertising for four main reasons: to counteract public hostility from ignorance or misinformation; to counter misleading information spread by critics and explain complex issues; to foster free-enterprise values; and to gain media access / counter perceived media bias.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these rationales to justify advocacy campaigns and to shape message strategy, but be aware that access does not equal persuasion — effectiveness varies by audience and context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Symmetric vs asymmetric purposes for issues campaigns
rubrics_metrics.description: An issues advertising campaign may be symmetric (two-way) or asymmetric depending on the organization's willingness to change or modify positions as a result of the debate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the organization has no intention of compromising, the campaign is likely asymmetric (one-way persuasion). If the organization is open to compromise, the campaign may be symmetric (participatory dialogue). This determines message tone and long-term engagement strategy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role of formative research and testing
rubrics_metrics.description: Before committing to a full advertising program, conduct formative research on sample publics to test message comprehension, appeal, and likely retention/acceptance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the research to select facts, craft copy, test headlines/art, estimate readership/viewership, and forecast realistic objectives (exposure vs acceptance). Formative research informs budgeting and media scheduling decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lobbying support activities (five basic areas)
rubrics_metrics.description: The typical lobbyist's work, similar to a PR practitioner, includes: establishing coalitions; doing research and preparing reports; making contacts with influential people; preparing witnesses and speakers; and focusing debate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Effective lobbying requires careful research (Congressional Record, CQ, Library of Congress resources), coalition-building among groups with overlapping interests while preserving identities, and preparation of materials (briefs, legislative analyses, draft legislation) that legislators and staff can use.

rubrics_metrics.name: Research and report preparation for lobbying
rubrics_metrics.description: Lobbyists must generate detailed, authoritative studies and reports to inform legislators and to fuel arguments for causes (e.g., state studies leading to congressional appropriations).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use sources such as Congressional Record, Congressional Quarterly, Library of Congress publications, Statistical Abstracts, and staff contacts. Good lobbyists are adept at using libraries/resources and preparing concise, usable materials (briefs, memos, draft legislation) for lawmakers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Establishing coalitions as a lobbying tactic
rubrics_metrics.description: To be effective, special interests often must combine efforts with other groups having similar goals, while managing overlapping priorities and preserving constituent identities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Coalitions can be ad hoc agreements to support specific legislation or institutionalized organizations with staff, offices, and newsletters. Broad, diverse coalitions appear more persuasive to legislators but constituent groups typically retain separate identities and agendas.
